cards.title: Handle first-step objections on the page, not just product objections
cards.summary: Identify and answer fears about requesting the CTA itself—uncertainty, embarrassment, being pitched—on the page before asking for contact details.
cards.use_when: When optimizing a lead capture page, quote form, or service CTA where visitors hesitate to make contact.
steps: Distinguish two objection types: objections to doing business with you (product, price, service fit) and objections to requesting the offer (the first step).

For conversion, surface the first-step objections: 'I don't know if you work with me,' 'I don't know what happens after I submit,' 'I fear embarrassment if I don't qualify,' 'I'll be spammed or pitched.'
Answer these on the page near the CTA in plain English.

Example: a construction free-quote page was a wash-out because nothing told visitors whether the business served them. A cycling claims page's 'start my claim' was too high commitment; 'find out if you could claim' or 'find out how much you could claim' would lower the step.
Target people on the edge, not those already ready to buy; the already-ready don't need conversion optimization.
caveats: The source does not prescribe a fixed number of objections to answer; validate fears with your audience.
cards.source_name: COMPLETE Revenue-increasing Conversion Rate Optimisation (CRO) Course.docx

cards.title: Remove fear of embarrassment from the CTA (the brownie analogy)
cards.summary: Like cocktail sticks signalling free samples, explicit permission and clear next-step signals reduce the embarrassment that kills conversion.
cards.use_when: When CTA wording or page context leaves visitors unsure whether the action is allowed, free, or safe.
steps: Identify where visitors might fear embarrassment: not qualifying, being sold to, committing too soon, being challenged.
Add 'cocktail sticks': explicit signals that the action is permitted and free—e.g., 'no obligation,' 'free,' 'find out if.'
Better still, state exactly what they get, like a sign saying 'try some of this delicious Fat Witch walnut brownie free of charge,' with an easy purchase path later.

Example: kitchen design CTA—'contact us now to arrange a free kitchen design and no obligation quote... if you'd like a free home survey, please include your address'—removes fears: no forced home visit, plain English, optional address.
Fear of embarrassment destroys conversion; make the next step obvious and inviting.
caveats: The elaborate Fat Witch example is aspirational; the source advises doing one thing at a time.
cards.source_name: COMPLETE Revenue-increasing Conversion Rate Optimisation (CRO) Course.docx

cards.title: Run the boiler-repair scenario to surface customer objections
cards.summary: A vivid scenario exercise puts you in the prospect's mindset to list the questions and objections they need answered before contacting you.
cards.use_when: Before writing CTA page copy or auditing a lead-gen page.
steps: Set the scenario: boiler faulty, newborn baby, dead of winter, you search 'boiler repair in my area.'
List every question/objection before you'd contact the first engineer: approximate cost, speed of arrival, reliability, qualifications, boiler type, service area.
Note the mistake: assuming people with questions will just contact you. Most do initial scouting; if they can't tell you're in the right ballpark, they leave.
Translate the list into page content that answers these before the CTA.
Then repeat for your own business: what questions would a prospect have?
caveats: Qualitative exercise; no required number of objections.
cards.source_name: COMPLETE Revenue-increasing Conversion Rate Optimisation (CRO) Course.docx

cards.title: List top three fears about requesting your CTA and counter each
cards.summary: Identify the three biggest fears prospects have about your CTA and write explicit counter-messaging for each near the action point.
cards.use_when: Writing or auditing a lead capture page, free consultation offer, or newsletter signup.
steps: Write the top three fears about requesting your CTA. For Exposure Ninja's free review: low value, nothing new, someone will pitch me.

Counter each: low value → cite 400+ five-star reviews; nothing new → 'a 15-minute personal video with a prioritized step-by-step plan'; pitched → 'video emailed to your address,' no salesperson meeting.
Use phrases: 'no obligation,' 'to see if we might be a good fit,' 'apply for a discovery call,' 'low pitch.'
For e-commerce newsletter discount: fear of spam → 'occasional tips on how to X' and valuable content.
Place counters where the visitor decides, not buried on another page.
caveats: Fears are audience-specific; validate with customers.
cards.source_name: COMPLETE Revenue-increasing Conversion Rate Optimisation (CRO) Course.docx

cards.title: Lower CTA commitment; don't take a step too far down the buyer journey
cards.summary: Choose CTA wording that matches the audience's stage—'find out if' or 'get a free quote' may beat 'start my claim' or 'book a survey'.
cards.use_when: Choosing button labels or offer framing for claims, services, or quote requests.
steps: Replace high-commitment 'start my claim' with 'find out if you could claim,' 'find out how much you could claim,' or 'try our 30-second claim checker.'
Explain technical terms by their outcome: 'free claim assessment' → 'to establish if you have a valid claim, your likelihood of winning, and possible compensation.'

For audiences who already know they need the service and want a price, 'get a free quote' may beat 'book a free survey' (ADT split test reported a 60% uplift; source gives no sample size, duration, or significance).
If the offer is simple, keep the CTA simple; don't force a bigger step.
caveats: The ADT result is an example, not a guaranteed benchmark; test with your audience.
cards.source_name: COMPLETE Revenue-increasing Conversion Rate Optimisation (CRO) Course.docx

cards.title: Use a multi-step form that starts with need/problem details
cards.summary: Asking about the problem first feels like a diagnosis; asking for contact details first feels like pure lead capture.
cards.use_when: Designing multi-step lead forms, claim checkers, or quote request flows.
steps: Order steps: step 1 injury/need details; step 2 personal details (name, email, phone); step 3 results.
Frame step 1 as diagnosis: the visitor invests before giving personal info, so step 2 feels less burdensome; use 'tell us where to send it.'
On the results step, set up human follow-up: 'someone will be in contact from the claims team to give your results'—this makes the follow-up call expected.
If results need human calculation, don't fake live results; explain that someone will be in touch.
On the CTA page, focus on getting the test done, not selling your firm.
caveats: Results may require human intervention; don't promise instant automated accuracy.
cards.source_name: COMPLETE Revenue-increasing Conversion Rate Optimisation (CRO) Course.docx

cards.title: Describe exactly what happens after the visitor submits
cards.summary: Spell out the post-submission process in plain English to remove fear of the unknown.
cards.use_when: Writing form page copy for consultations, quotes, or surveys.
steps: Use wording like: 'For a free no obligation consultation, fill in the details below and one of our team will be in touch to arrange a consultation at a time of your convenience via phone, Skype or in person.'
This handles: no office visit required, confidential, convenient time, choice of medium.
For free site surveys, say 'free quote' if a home visit isn't required (ADT example).
If the process is long, in-person, risky, or has serious objections, explain the exact process on the page where you ask for the lead.
Kitchen design example: 'If you'd like to arrange a free home survey, please don't forget to include your home address'—address is optional.
caveats: Match wording to the actual process; don't promise channels you don't offer.
cards.source_name: COMPLETE Revenue-increasing Conversion Rate Optimisation (CRO) Course.docx

cards.title: Build social proof for the CTA itself, not just the business
cards.summary: Collect and display reviews/testimonials about your free offer or lead magnet right where you ask people to request it.
cards.use_when: When a free review, consultation, newsletter, or lead magnet is the conversion goal.
steps: After delivering the free thing, ask for a review of that thing. Email: 'If you found this review useful, please consider giving us a review on Google/Facebook.'
For a consultation, ask leavers: 'Other people thinking of getting a free consultation—what would you say to them?'
Collect newsletter ratings via NPS tools (source names Delighted; verify current interface).
Display these offer-specific reviews on the page advertising the offer, especially near CTA and above the fold.
Exposure Ninja's review page sells the review, not the agency; testimonials are reviews of the review service.
caveats: Tool names and interfaces change; verify before implementation.
cards.source_name: COMPLETE Revenue-increasing Conversion Rate Optimisation (CRO) Course.docx

cards.title: Review volume can beat average rating in buying decisions
cards.summary: People often choose the option with more reviews even if the average rating is worse, so build review volume over time.
cards.use_when: Building a social proof strategy for a product, service, or CTA.
steps: Use the Amazon two-books example: most people buy the book with more reviews even when average rating is lower.
Send review links to Google My Business, Trustpilot, Amazon, or your site after positive interactions.
If new, use the reviews you have (even two customers) but aim to accumulate volume.
Position reviews where trust is asked: above the fold and next to CTAs. National Accident Helpline puts Trustpilot reviews above the fold and again beside the CTA.
caveats: Source presents this as consumer tendency, not universal law; context and industry matter.
cards.source_name: COMPLETE Revenue-increasing Conversion Rate Optimisation (CRO) Course.docx

cards.title: Make the CTA the most visible element on the page
cards.summary: Follow familiar e-commerce layouts with a prominent CTA box, big buttons, white space, and repeated CTAs.
cards.use_when: Layout and visibility optimization for lead-gen or ecommerce pages.
steps: Place a bordered CTA box on the top right (desktop) with a big button and surrounding white space.
Repeat the same CTA in header, banner, phone number, sticky footer, and live chat widget as appropriate.
Avoid burying the CTA at the bottom; imagine Amazon doing that and how badly it would perform.
Example: a client site with many CTAs converted at 9.2% in its first month vs 2.48% for the previous site (source says after adding conversion tools; not a benchmark promise).
Make it obvious what visitors are supposed to do.
caveats: Case study result is an example; use conventions unless you have a tested reason to break them.
cards.source_name: COMPLETE Revenue-increasing Conversion Rate Optimisation (CRO) Course.docx

cards.title: Assume visitors are busy, distracted, and unfamiliar (Homer Simpson rule)
cards.summary: Even sophisticated audiences behave like distracted novices on a new site; prioritize familiarity around conversion paths.
cards.use_when: When stakeholders push for unique navigation, menus, or CTA designs.
steps: Watch user testing videos; expect people to miss obvious CTAs and describe them as dumb or lazy.
Remember everyone is busy and distracted; unfamiliarity makes your site look confusing.
Avoid pioneering new UI patterns around the conversion path. If you must teach people to use your site, you'll have a bad time.
Example: an award-winning creative legal site had massive bounce because its hamburger menu wasn't recognizable; the menu was the first thing to go.
Make important areas look familiar; you can be creative elsewhere.
caveats: Source acknowledges times to stand out, but not in core conversion UI.
cards.source_name: COMPLETE Revenue-increasing Conversion Rate Optimisation (CRO) Course.docx

cards.title: Balance form field count: too few can also lower conversion
cards.summary: Conversion falls as fields increase from 3 to 10, but 1–2 fields can feel like pure lead capture; add enough to feel like a diagnosis.
cards.use_when: Designing lead forms and deciding how much information to request.
steps: Reference the HubSpot study: conversion declines from 3 to 10 fields.
But 1–2 fields (phone only, or name+email) signal 'we'll just pitch you,' lowering conversion.
Add fields that make the form feel like a diagnosis (injury details, claim type, budget) with perceived value.
Use suppression deliberately if you must filter unqualified leads. Exposure Ninja asks more questions because free reviews cost time and money; it filters non-serious people.
Don't suppress so much that you lose your perfect client.
caveats: HubSpot data is cited from source; exact study conditions aren't given; test on your audience.
cards.source_name: COMPLETE Revenue-increasing Conversion Rate Optimisation (CRO) Course.docx

cards.title: Prefer multiple-choice/dropdowns over text areas; ask only what you'll use
cards.summary: Text areas reduce conversion dramatically; use multiple choice/dropdowns and only request information you actually use.
cards.use_when: Form field design and lead qualification.
steps: Convert questions to multiple choice or dropdown where possible; text areas lower conversion.
Ask the minimum information needed to proceed in the sales process.
Newsletter: ask name and email; birthday can enable personalized offers; just email may lift conversion but lower open rates.
Service: ask phone only if you'll call; otherwise omit or make optional.
Ask qualifying/disqualifying info (e.g., budget ranges) if your sales team can't handle all leads.
Never ask for information you won't use.
caveats: Some questions may require free text; source says 'if possible'.
cards.source_name: COMPLETE Revenue-increasing Conversion Rate Optimisation (CRO) Course.docx

cards.title: Choose the right format for delivering your free result
cards.summary: Compare call/Zoom, in-person, email presentation, and full trial; each trades off scalability, risk, and feedback.
cards.use_when: Designing the deliverable of your free offer or lead magnet.
steps: Phone/Skype/Zoom call: good for testing and live feedback; allows qualification. Exposure Ninja used calls first to learn what reviews needed.

In-person: least scalable but often effective for high ticket; discovery days (6–10 people) can add scale. Challenge the assumption it's always needed: Exposure Ninja has £10k/month clients it never met.
Email presentation (video, proposal, mockup): lowest risk for prospect; they do nothing and can ignore it; can set up follow-up.

Trial of full product: beware onboarding burden; users may balk at setup (CRM example). Make onboarding painless or game-like, step-by-step. Compare Infusionsoft (setup fee increases commitment) vs Zoho (free trial) — no universal rule; test audience.
caveats: Examples are situational; no single best format.
cards.source_name: COMPLETE Revenue-increasing Conversion Rate Optimisation (CRO) Course.docx

cards.title: Script sales calls and seed your service throughout the free deliverable
cards.summary: Script calls (even as key questions), do the process yourself first, and mention your paid service early, with case studies throughout, and next step at the end.
cards.use_when: Turning leads into buyers from free consultations, reviews, or audits.
steps: Do the sales process yourself first to find what works, then give the script to your team.
A script can be five questions to answer during the call, plus the next step; it doesn't mean rigid word-for-word.
Seed the product/service: at start say you work with clients helping with X; use case studies throughout; at end state the next step to work with you.
Reason: people used to ask 'do you actually do this for people?' because the service was never mentioned.
Address what the lead is most scared of immediately: e.g., 'this is not a pitch'; for spam fear, offer email frequency choice.
caveats: Script needs flexibility for off-script questions.
cards.source_name: COMPLETE Revenue-increasing Conversion Rate Optimisation (CRO) Course.docx

cards.title: Reframe existing sales-process steps as the free offer
cards.summary: Look at your existing process; an already-provided free consultation or visual can be advertised as the benefit instead of adding new free work.
cards.use_when: When your team worries about giving too much away or lacks a lead magnet.
steps: Walk through your sales process.
Identify steps you already provide free (e.g., 30-minute call, 3D visual) that aren't advertised.
Reframe as the stated benefit: 'request a free consultation and we'll help you X' or 'free 3D visual mockup.'
Example: an exhibition stand company already did free 3D visuals but didn't advertise it; advertising it attracted more leads.
Ask what clear and attractive next step you offer; if you can't say how it moves people closer to their goals, it's not compelling enough.
caveats: Check cost of existing free steps before scaling.
cards.source_name: COMPLETE Revenue-increasing Conversion Rate Optimisation (CRO) Course.docx

cards.title: Assess whether a high sales close rate reflects a narrow lead funnel
cards.summary: Widening the funnel brings more unqualified leads and lowers sales conversion percentage—that's expected; have a plan B.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a sales-assisted or lead-generation journey; this is not a rule for ecommerce checkout conversion.
steps: Treat the presenter's high-close-rate claim as a hypothesis: compare qualified lead volume, sales capacity and acquisition economics before broadening the funnel.
If sales conversion rate is very high (near 100%), the marketing funnel is too narrow; you're only getting self-qualified leads.
Widen the funnel; expect more unqualified leads; conversion percentage may drop.
Have a plan B for unqualified leads (nurture, different offer, disqualify).
Example: IT support company got more leads but lower sales conversion; source called it expected/perfect.
Don't aim for 100% sales conversion; it signals not enough persuasion at the top.
caveats: Source asserts no 100% conversion is a red flag; no numeric target for ideal rate.
A high close rate alone does not prove the funnel is too narrow. Do not broaden acquisition solely to lower this percentage.
cards.source_name: COMPLETE Revenue-increasing Conversion Rate Optimisation (CRO) Course.docx
